nameStory: The tench gets its common name from the Old French word 'tenche,' which comes from the Latin 'tinca.' Interestingly, it's also called the 'doctor fish' because other fish were once believed to rub against tench to heal their wounds with the tench's thick, protective slime coating!
description: The tench is a thick-bodied, olive-green freshwater fish with a distinctive barbel (whisker-like projection) at each corner of its mouth. Originally from Europe and Asia, this hardy fish has established small populations in some New England waters. Tench typically grow 12-16 inches long and have a robust, almost cylindrical body shape with very small scales that feel smooth and slippery to the touch.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Deep, thick body that feels solid and muscular when handled, with a rounded belly and back that gives it an almost barrel-like appearance

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Dark olive-green to bronze coloration that can appear almost black in muddy water, with a lighter yellowish belly

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small barbels (fleshy whiskers) at each corner of the mouth that feel soft and flexible - a key identifying feature

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Rounded fins with no spines, and a distinctive square-cut tail fin that lacks the deep fork of many other fish

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in slow-moving or still waters with muddy bottoms and heavy vegetation, often in areas other fish avoid

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized fish typically 12-16 inches long with very small, embedded scales that create an almost leather-like skin texture

habitat: In New England, tench are found in a few quiet ponds, slow-moving rivers, and heavily vegetated lake areas with soft, muddy bottoms. They prefer shallow, weedy areas where the water is still or barely moving, often in places with thick aquatic vegetation and low oxygen levels that would stress other fish species.

seasonality.spring: Tench become more active as water warms and may be spotted near shallow, weedy areas preparing for spawning season. Look for them in muddy shallows during warmer spring days.
seasonality.summer: Most active season when tench spawn among aquatic plants, creating yellow, sticky egg masses on vegetation. This is the best time to spot them as they move into very shallow water.
seasonality.fall: Activity decreases as water cools, and tench begin moving to deeper areas. They may still be caught but are less likely to be seen near the surface.
seasonality.winter: Tench become nearly dormant, burying themselves partially in soft mud at the bottom of ponds and lakes, making them almost impossible to observe.

funFact: Tench can survive in water with incredibly low oxygen levels that would kill most other fish - they can even live buried in mud for months during winter, essentially hibernating like a bear!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with small carp, but tench have the telltale barbels at the mouth corners (not under the mouth like carp) and a much more olive-green coloration. Remember: corner barbels = tench, under-mouth barbels = carp.
contextualKnowledge: Tench are not native to North America and are quite rare in New England waters. Any sighting is noteworthy since they represent small, established populations from historical introductions. They're considered exotic species but are not currently invasive.
compareHints: As the only member of the tench family in New England, compare tench to carp family members. Unlike common carp, tench have barbels only at the mouth corners, smoother-feeling scales, and prefer muddier, more stagnant waters. Tench also lack the carp's distinctive forked tail and have a more uniformly dark coloration.
